bull_bear.title: Management quality / tone

bull_bear.body: Management explicitly stated Century Ports provides no direct cost savings to the Ply business but serves as a separate profit center; Old Particle Board technology being completely scrapped rather than repurposed; Outsourcing in Plywood being phased out entirely for quality control despite capacity constraints.
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- The capex cycle has been debt-funded: Total Debt rose from Rs 239.07 crores (2022-23) to Rs 656.52, Rs 1,383.12, Rs 1,531.26 crores and Rs 1,644.21 crores at Q1 26-27, taking Total Debt/Equity from 0.16 to 0.65.
- Leverage metrics peaked with the build and are now easing: Total Debt/EBITDA went 0.52 (2022-23) to 1.27, 2.97 (2024-25), 2.47 (2025-26) and 2.20 (Q1 26-27); Interest Cover fell from 31.15 to a low of 4.15 in 2025-26 before recovering to 4.93.
- Returns are still far below the pre-capex level: Return on Avg Equity went 24.52% (2022-23) to 10.37% (2024-25), recovering to 13.09% (2025-26) and 13.52% (Q1 26-27); Return on Avg Capital Employed went 30.91% to 12.30%, then 13.43% and 14.39%.
- The debt mix has shifted from import-linked to bank funding: Capex Buyers' Credit fell from Rs 378.71 crores (2024-25) to Rs 232.52 crores (Q1 26-27) while Short Term Debt (From Banks) rose from Rs 538.11 crores to Rs 811.79 crores; there is no debt from related parties and no foreign-currency long-term debt in any year shown.
- Cash is run thin against this debt - Cash, Bank & Liquid Funds fell from Rs 278.21 crores (2022-23) to Rs 49.14 crores (2024-25) and stood at Rs 82.32 crores at Q1 26-27.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation policy (investor deck)

bull_bear.body:
- Strong brand recognition and market leadership, translating into sustained profitability through deep customer trust and loyalty
- Retained its leadership position in the plywood segment during the year, with plywood capacity utilisation at 94%
- Broad and versatile product portfolio spanning plywood, laminates, MDF, particle board, veneers, doors and composites, allowing it to cater to diverse consumer preferences across multiple segments
- Nationwide footprint and a robust distribution network reaching 28 States, 7 Union Territories and 695 districts, ensuring reliable product availability and uninterrupted supply
- Strategically positioned manufacturing facilities that enhance operational efficiency and enable quicker deliveries
- Operates in industries characterised by high entry barriers, supporting a durable competitive advantage and a well-protected market position
- Raw-material security from agroforestry: ~98% of primary timber sourced through agroforestry/farm forestry practices in the wood-based divisions
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Macro-economic risk — exposure to national and global economic fluctuations outside the Company's control — Named as the leading risk in the MD&A's 'mitigation of our prominent risks, 2025-26' table. Potential consequences flagged by management are possible erosion of brand relevance within the sector and region, growth momentum slowing or stagnating, and weakened overall competitiveness. Management rates the likelihood of sustained occurrence as Low, pointing to India as the world's sixth-largest economy with a steadily narrowing rural gap as the offsetting external stimulus.
- Timber raw-material availability and sourcing concentration — Structural for a timber-based industry: management itself identifies dependence on timber as a key raw material as the rationale for its Sustainable Forest / Plantation Management material issue. Roughly 98% of primary timber comes from agroforestry/farm forestry plantations, so the input base is concentrated in one sourcing model. The Company has responded by diversifying imports of plywood timber from Vietnam, Brazil and Africa to mitigate domestic supply constraints and price volatility, and by distributing over 78 Lac saplings with plantation training to secure future supply.
- Climate change, energy costs and GHG regulation — Flagged in the BRSR material-issues table as both risk and opportunity. Physical risks — floods, droughts and forest fires — can impair raw-material availability for the industry, while stringent renewable-energy regulation and volatile energy costs pose financial and operational risks that could affect operations and profitability. Financial implication stated as negative on the cost of transitioning to cleaner technologies. Mitigation is renewable integration (18% of total electricity consumption in FY 2025-26, up 62% YoY, on ~14.26 MW of installed solar plus a renewable PPA at the Chennai facilities), efficiency upgrades, biomass thermic fluid heaters and electric forklifts.
- Chemical management — adhesives, resins and formaldehyde exposure — Use of adhesives, resins and other chemicals in plywood manufacturing poses environmental and occupational health risks, and regulatory non-compliance can lead to legal liabilities. Stated financial implications are negative through compliance costs and potential regulatory fines. Mitigated through turbo air ventilators and exhaust fans, closed-loop chemical transfer pipelines and low-formaldehyde-emission binder resins.
- Responsible supply-chain / vendor conduct risk — Sourcing from suppliers engaged in unethical practices such as child labour, forced labour or non-compliance with environmental regulations is identified as a significant risk to the Company's values and brand reputation, with any association capable of causing operational disruptions and loss of stakeholder trust. Assessment currently rests on supplier ESG screening and a vendor evaluation form covering environmental aspects, with 75.85% of input material by value sourced from within India and 43.36% directly from MSMEs/small producers.
- Leverage and interest cover deteriorating as the expansion programme is debt-funded — Interest coverage ratio fell from 11.96 times to 7.57 times, which management attributes mainly to reduction in EBIT and higher interest expense on account of increased debt taken to fund ongoing expansions. Set against a large committed pipeline (Hoshiarpur, Uttar Pradesh and Odisha facilities to be commissioned in phases over the next few years), this is the structural financial risk carried into FY27. EBIT margin fell to 9.26% from 10.65% and return on net worth to 10.79% from 12.32% over the same period.
- Project-execution risk across a multi-state, multi-phase expansion pipeline — Management's own framework emphasises vigilant oversight across every stage of the project lifecycle — planning, development, execution and long-term sustainability — with specific protocols established for project-related risks. The pipeline still requires feasibility studies, statutory approvals and clearances and other pre-implementation activities before commissioning, so timeline and cost slippage is the live exposure.

business.body: The Company and its subsidiaries manufacture and trade plywood and allied products, decorative laminates, veneers, doors, composites, medium density fibre board (MDF) and particle board, and also operate Container Freight Station (CFS) services; manufacturing and trading account for 97% of turnover and CFS services for the balance 3%. It operates predominantly through a B2B model, supplying in bulk to authorised distributors and dealers who in turn serve wholesalers, architects, interior designers, builders, contractors and furniture manufacturers. It also sells to institutional customers such as real estate developers, large-scale furniture manufacturers and government departments, and to export customers across Asia, the Middle East, North America, South America, Europe, Africa and Oceania.

outlook.title: Growth verticals / optionality

outlook.body:
- Capacity-led growth through greenfield expansion: a commissioned particle board plant at Tiruvallur, a plywood unit at Hoshiarpur nearing completion, and Board-approved plywood/MDF/particle board facilities in Uttar Pradesh and Odisha, sited for proximity to raw material, skilled manpower, logistics and large customer markets.
- Operating part of the business through subsidiaries, established directly or as step-down entities or via acquisition of majority stake, described explicitly as a strategic measure.
- Scaling the wholly-owned subsidiary Century Panels Ltd's laminate, MDF and PVC operations at the Gopavaram facility in Kadapa District, Andhra Pradesh, with expansion of the PVC plant underway.
- Using international certifications at Century Panels (IMS - ISO 9001, 14001, 45001; FSC; Greenguard (US); BIS 2046; Malaysian and Singaporean CGS standards) as the platform for entering new geographies and expanding the export footprint via the MDF and Laminate divisions.
- Premiumisation and new-category product development — new categories such as Table Tops and Kitchen Tops, plus premium value-added products like White Colour Core and specialty compact fibre boards; in the parent, development and commercialisation of CenBoil Plus (970 kg/m³), a high-density AWR-grade product.
- Automation and digital integration across manufacturing: IoT and SCADA-based production monitoring across plywood, laminate, veneer composing, calibrator and energy plant operations; machine breakdown alerts integrated with SAP S/4HANA; QR code-based traceability in branding machines.
- Energy cost and carbon reduction as an operating lever: wood waste and agricultural residue bio-fuel in thermic fluid heating, continued augmentation of rooftop solar across manufacturing units, VFDs, APFC and Energy Management Systems for machine-wise electricity monitoring, and heat recovery systems.
- In-house R&D and technology absorption — H308.83 Lac spent on R&D in FY 2025-26 focused on product development, process optimisation, quality, energy efficiency and sustainable manufacturing; imported technologies (Automatic Mat Putty Line, additional STEINEMANN sanding head, EVO Fuge 360 Steam Recovery System) fully integrated.
- Workforce capability building through regular training in industrial electrical systems and safety, Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning applications, quality management and operational excellence.
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: FY 2025-26 was a build-out year funded partly by incremental debt. The greenfield Particle Board project at Tiruvallur, Tamil Nadu (240,000 CBM per annum) started commercial production during the year and is now operational, lifting particle board volumes 53.4% to 1,07,500 cbm against a 67% capacity utilisation. The greenfield plywood unit at Hoshiarpur, Punjab — 60,000 CBM per annum at an estimated capital outlay of H180 Crore — is at an advanced stage of implementation, targeted at North India demand and the region's agro-forestry ecosystem, with commercial production expected by the third quarter of FY 2026-27. Beyond that, the Company is setting up a plywood and MDF facility in Uttar Pradesh (plywood 60,000 CBM per annum in Phase I at approximately H200 Crore, a further 30,000 CBM per annum in Phase II at approximately H130 Crore, and an MDF line of 330,000 CBM per annum at approximately H800 Crore), and the Board has approved an Odisha facility for plywood and Particle Board/MDF (60,000 CBM per annum of plywood in each of Phase I and Phase II at approximately H230 Crore and H140 Crore respectively, plus a 240,000 CBM per annum Particle Board/MDF plant at approximately H500 Crore). Both sites were chosen for proximity to raw material sources, skilled manpower, logistics and infrastructure, and access to large customer markets; feasibility studies, statutory approvals and pre-implementation activities are in progress and commissioning is expected in phases over the next few years. Existing utilisation at year-end was 94% in plywood, 84% in laminates, 82% in MDF and 67% in particle board. The cost of the build-out is visible in the accounts: interest coverage fell from 11.96 times to 7.57 times, which management attributes partly to higher interest expense on increased debt taken to fund ongoing expansions. Management frames the whole programme against a stated goal of achieving revenues of H12,000 crore by 2031. Note on quantum: the only capital-expenditure figures supplied as a named disclosure (segment note, pages 328/399/400) are flagged ambiguous with no unit printed, so no rupee capex quantum is reportable from this bundle.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- India positioned as the fastest-growing major economy — real GDP grew 7.7% in FY26 vs 7.1% in FY25, with the World Bank revising its FY27 growth estimate to approximately 6.6%.
- Growth expected to be shaped by strong domestic demand and resilient private consumption, supported by low inflation and GST rationalisation, alongside stable export performance with improved access to key markets.
- Global backdrop management works against: IMF projects global growth at 3.0% in 2026 recovering to 3.4% in 2027, with global inflation rising to 4.7% in 2026 before easing to 3.9% in 2027, leaving the outlook vulnerable to prolonged conflict and commodity price volatility.
- Indian furniture market valued at approximately USD 25.4 billion in 2025 and expected to reach USD 44.3 billion by 2034 (6.4% CAGR), propelled by rising disposable incomes, urbanisation and housing/real estate expansion.
- Indian plywood market valued at over USD 7 billion in 2025, with commercial ply at a 58% share; real estate developers and modular furniture makers prefer calibrated BWP grade plywood, and stricter E0 and E1 formaldehyde emission norms are boosting demand for low-emission plywood in premium projects.
- Indian decorative laminates market around USD 2 billion in 2025, with the industry shifting towards premium and value-added products, textured finishes and sustainable materials; renovation cycles accelerating on nuclear family formation and social-media-driven design awareness.
- Indian MDF market around USD 1.4 billion in 2025, projected to grow at a high single-digit CAGR over the next five years; Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana targeting 2 crore urban homes by 2030 generates structural demand at approximately 0.22 m³ of MDF per unit, and IS 12440:2025 boosts local sourcing while curbing imports.
- Structural formalisation of the panel industry: the furniture quality control order enforced from February 2026 and BIS Quality Control Orders are reshaping compliance and pushing unorganised producers to certify, widening access to government and institutional demand.
- Real estate as the demand backbone — market size expected to expand from ~US$ 200 billion in 2021 to US$ 1 trillion by 2030, with premiumisation evident as homes priced above H1 crore accounted for nearly 63% of total sales value versus 53% the previous year.
- Long-horizon consumption drivers cited by management: more than 40% of India's population urban by 2030, consumer spending projected at USD 4.3 trillion by 2030, and 1.04 billion working-age individuals by 2030 shifting preference from traditional carpentry to wood panels.
- Company-specific positioning: 'Supported by strong brand recognition, a diversified product portfolio and an extensive distribution network, the Company remains well positioned to capitalise on the long-term growth opportunities in the decorative laminates segment.'
- Margin levers flagged by management: energy and thermal consumption reduction, lower operating costs and improved resource utilisation, reduced waste generation and rejection rates from the year's technology-absorption initiatives.

risks.note: Named as the leading risk in the MD&A's 'mitigation of our prominent risks, 2025-26' table. Potential consequences flagged by management are possible erosion of brand relevance within the sector and region, growth momentum slowing or stagnating, and weakened overall competitiveness. Management rates the likelihood of sustained occurrence as Low, pointing to India as the world's sixth-largest economy with a steadily narrowing rural gap as the offsetting external stimulus.
risks.risk: Macro-economic risk — exposure to national and global economic fluctuations outside the Company's control

risks.note: Structural for a timber-based industry: management itself identifies dependence on timber as a key raw material as the rationale for its Sustainable Forest / Plantation Management material issue. Roughly 98% of primary timber comes from agroforestry/farm forestry plantations, so the input base is concentrated in one sourcing model. The Company has responded by diversifying imports of plywood timber from Vietnam, Brazil and Africa to mitigate domestic supply constraints and price volatility, and by distributing over 78 Lac saplings with plantation training to secure future supply.
risks.risk: Timber raw-material availability and sourcing concentration

risks.note: Flagged in the BRSR material-issues table as both risk and opportunity. Physical risks — floods, droughts and forest fires — can impair raw-material availability for the industry, while stringent renewable-energy regulation and volatile energy costs pose financial and operational risks that could affect operations and profitability. Financial implication stated as negative on the cost of transitioning to cleaner technologies. Mitigation is renewable integration (18% of total electricity consumption in FY 2025-26, up 62% YoY, on ~14.26 MW of installed solar plus a renewable PPA at the Chennai facilities), efficiency upgrades, biomass thermic fluid heaters and electric forklifts.
risks.risk: Climate change, energy costs and GHG regulation

risks.note: Use of adhesives, resins and other chemicals in plywood manufacturing poses environmental and occupational health risks, and regulatory non-compliance can lead to legal liabilities. Stated financial implications are negative through compliance costs and potential regulatory fines. Mitigated through turbo air ventilators and exhaust fans, closed-loop chemical transfer pipelines and low-formaldehyde-emission binder resins.
risks.risk: Chemical management — adhesives, resins and formaldehyde exposure

risks.note: Sourcing from suppliers engaged in unethical practices such as child labour, forced labour or non-compliance with environmental regulations is identified as a significant risk to the Company's values and brand reputation, with any association capable of causing operational disruptions and loss of stakeholder trust. Assessment currently rests on supplier ESG screening and a vendor evaluation form covering environmental aspects, with 75.85% of input material by value sourced from within India and 43.36% directly from MSMEs/small producers.

Interest coverage ratio fell from 11.96 times to 7.57 times, which management attributes mainly to reduction in EBIT and higher interest expense on account of increased debt taken to fund ongoing expansions. Set against a large committed pipeline (Hoshiarpur, Uttar Pradesh and Odisha facilities to be commissioned in phases over the next few years), this is the structural financial risk carried into FY27. EBIT margin fell to 9.26% from 10.65% and return on net worth to 10.79% from 12.32% over the same period.
risks.risk: Leverage and interest cover deteriorating as the expansion programme is debt-funded

risks.note: Management's own framework emphasises vigilant oversight across every stage of the project lifecycle — planning, development, execution and long-term sustainability — with specific protocols established for project-related risks. The pipeline still requires feasibility studies, statutory approvals and clearances and other pre-implementation activities before commissioning, so timeline and cost slippage is the live exposure.
risks.risk: Project-execution risk across a multi-state, multi-phase expansion pipeline
